answer:
These days, English is almost impossible to avoid in everyday life. We hear it on television and in song lyrics, study it at school, and often use it at work. This constant exposure gives us a fairly good feel for how the language works. I think most people understand at least some English, and many probably have an excellent command of it. When I consider my own abilities, however, some areas are clearly more challenging than others. I feel more confident in the receptive skills of reading and listening than in writing and speaking.

Throughout my years of studying English, first at primary school and then at secondary school, my teachers placed a strong emphasis on writing. In secondary school in particular, we wrote numerous essays and reviews. Yet despite all this practice, I still encounter difficulties when writing in English. Spelling can sometimes be a challenge, but I find grammar more troublesome. In my experience, grammatical problems are often complicated and difficult to resolve, whereas the spelling of a word can easily be checked in a dictionary.

We did not get much reading practice at school. Although we had textbooks, the articles in them were often very short and covered unrelated topics, which made them seem disconnected and out of context. Put simply, the textbooks were boring. We also read several works of literature and wrote reviews of them. I think reading literature is an enormously rewarding way to develop greater fluency in a language. The reading skills I acquired also proved useful in my religious studies courses, where much of the required reading was in English.

My greatest difficulty when reading English arises when a text contains specialised language. Reading something in English that I would probably struggle to understand even in Swedish is a real challenge, as well as being very time-consuming. This brings me to another problem: my patience, or rather my lack of it. Naturally, reading in English takes longer than reading in Swedish, at least initially, but for some reason I find that difficult to accept.

Speaking and listening are obviously closely related. Even so, I find listening the easiest of the four language skills and speaking the most difficult. This is undoubtedly partly because I get far more practice listening, especially through television and music, than I do speaking. Although I do not understand every word, I can usually follow the overall meaning without difficulty. Specialised language, however, presents problems when listening just as it does when reading.

As I mentioned earlier, speaking is the aspect of English I find most challenging. I have had little practical experience of speaking the language, as I have never spent an extended period abroad. English teaching at school focused primarily, if not exclusively, on theory, so I had few opportunities to practise speaking there either. If anything, school can make you even more reluctant to speak: you become so concerned about getting the grammar right that you are afraid to open your mouth for fear of being laughed at. I know this sounds rather bleak, and it may not reflect everyone’s experience. Still, I believe these fears would soon fade with regular speaking practice.

Now that I have completed this assignment, I realise how difficult it is to assess my own abilities in the four language skills. I have never had trouble getting good grades in English, but I firmly believe that grades rarely reflect what someone actually knows. What I do know is that learning a language involves many different skills, and I would like to improve in all of them.
